item.title: US singer D4vd to go on trial for murder in death of 14-year-old
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c70gkg62w0ro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US singer D4vd to go on trial for murder in death of 14-year-old - Published A judge has ruled that US musician D4vd will go on trial for murder over the death of a teenage girl. The decision came after a five-day preliminary hearing, in which Los Angeles prosecutors questioned a dozen witnesses and displayed graphic photographic evidence as 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez's family watched on. The star, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke, is accused of killing the girl, whose remains were found last September in a Tesla registered to his address. Burke, 21, has pleaded not guilty to charges of murdering and sexually abusing her. Burke is scheduled to be in court next on 31 August to have the charges against him formally read. The trial is to start within 90 days of that date. The charges include first-degree murder, mutilation of human remains and child sexual abuse. The murder charges include special circumstances linked to financial gain that could make Burke potentially liable for the death sentence. Prosecutors have alleged Burke stabbed the teen before dismembering her body after years of sexual abuse. The accusation of murder for financial gain is among the special circumstances included in the charges making Burke potentially liable for the death sentence. They allege he killed her because the teen had threatened to reveal his relationship with a minor and destroy his multi-million dollar music career. Evidence read in court on Monday showed threats Hernandez made to Burke on 22 April 2025, stemming from arguments about his friendship with another girl. "I swear to GOD I will kill u", one expletive-laden text said, followed by a threat to strangle him and tell her dad lies about him. "i will end ur career and ur life I will damage anything," the text went on. The following day, Hernandez went to Burke's Hollywood home in an Uber he had sent to pick her up. Prosecutors alleged that Burke stabbed her once she arrived. During questioning at the hearing on Monday, Detective Corey Farrell of the Los Angeles Police Department said text messages indicated that the defendant and the girl had attended church with her family. In response to the defence, the detective said he was aware the teen had misrepresented her age to the defendant, telling him she was 16 and 18 at different times. Burke's defence lawyers argued there was not sufficient evidence that he had committed the crime. They said her parents were aware of what was going on between them and had even given written consent for her to travel to London with Burke for a week. The defence highlighted texts on the 22nd and the 23rd of April that suggested Celeste had insisted on going to Burke's Hollywood Hills home and that he had argued against her coming before agreeing to send her an Uber on the night of the 23rd. He "repeatedly expressed love and care for Ms Hernandez after they broke up", defence attorney Marilyn Bednarski said in court. The medical examiner's inability to prove how the two penetrating wounds found in the girl occurred and the lack of surveillance video capturing Burke being home on the night of 23 April showed a lack of evidence, the defence argued. Los Angeles County Superior Court Judge Charlaine Olmedo ruled that evidence presented during the preliminary hearing provided probable cause for a trial. Burke is charged with murder, continuous sexual abuse of a child under 14, and unlawful mutilation of human remains. "The people have met their burden on all counts," Judge Olmedo said. She found that prosecutors met the threshold for the charge of murder with special circumstances, including lying in wait, motive for financial gain and eliminating a witness. Following the hearing, Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said his office only presented a fraction of the evidence it had against Burke, and that it would present everything in the coming trial. Hochman also said his office had not yet determined if it would pursue the death penalty against Burke. Listen to the BBC's Fame Under Fire podcast which brings you the latest from inside the Los Angeles courtroom at the D4vd preliminary hearing. Gruesome images of the girl's dismembered corpse were shown in court during the preliminary hearing. A homicide detective testified that Burke had ordered a body bag, chainsaws, an inflatable pool and a shovel online in the days after Celeste's death. Prosecutors highlighted records that revealed Burke ordered chainsaws and a shovel to his residence after April 23. They allege he used a chainsaw to dismember Hernadez's body. However, Los Angeles Police Department criminalist Lauren Wallace testified that the chainsaws found in his garage tested negative for the presence of blood and were not tested for DNA thereafter, a point the defence highlighted in their attempt to prove the evidence presented was inconclusive. However, investigators were unable to locate a third, 10-inch Makita chainsaw, which prosecutors claim Burke also ordered following Hernandez's death.

item.title: Number of suspects in fatal Seattle food festival shooting rises to three
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c78gjyx4q2yo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Number of suspects in fatal Seattle food festival shooting rises to three - Published Seattle police say they now believe at least three people were involved in a fatal shooting at a food festival on Sunday. Police initially said two suspects were thought to have been shooting at each other at the annual Bite of Seattle food festival at the Space Needle - one of the city's most popular tourist spots. However, court papers relating to the arrest of one of these, a 15-year-old, on Monday revealed they now think there is a third attacker. One is still being sought by police, while the other is thought to have been killed at the scene. Three people were killed in the shooting and at least four others were injured, including a two-year old boy. The teenage suspect waived his initial appearance in court on Monday, and he was remanded in custody pending trial, according to local media. Ahead of the hearing, police revealed in court documents that they believe that three suspects may have fired shots during the "gunfight". Court papers filed by the police say investigators are searching for "at least one other unknown suspect", according to local media. Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson, speaking at a news conference on Monday, said: "Police continue to look for a third possible suspect." The three people who died on Sunday were 19-year-old Junior Cee Niko Semo, Carlos Israel Sanchez Villalba, 44, and Ashley Whitehead, 56, according to the King County medical examiner. Police now believe that Semo was involved in the gunfight. Two deaths were confirmed at the scene, and one person died in hospital. Two guns were recovered at the scene, police said. Speaking on Monday afternoon, Assistant Police Chief Nicole Powell said that preliminary information indicated the shooting may have been "gang-related". She added that the 15-year-old suspect and the 19-year-old who was killed are believed to be "associated with each other". She declined to describe their connection. Sunday was the final day of the annual three-day free food festival, which draws some 350,000 people each year. Videos shared online showed people crouched on the ground, taking cover behind pillars and shelves of merchandise in the Space Needle's lobby during the shooting. Leanne Coles, another witness, told CBS News, the BBC's US partner: "Everybody started running, and so we just ran too, and we ran through the garden and we ducked and we decided to keep running with the crowd." Faith Adia Hunter told the Associated Press news agency that one of the shooters was near her and her friends when they heard the shots, sending them fleeing for shelter in the Seattle Children's Museum. "We were right next to him when it started so we took off running," she said. Washington Governor Bob Ferguson said on social media: "My prayers are with the families of the victims, and the responders as they work to keep people safe." Mayor Wilson also condemned the shooting as an "act of horrific violence". Related topics - Published3 days ago

item.title: Shots fired at US consulate in Toronto for a second time this year
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgvnw44rz9o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Shots fired at US consulate in Toronto for a second time this year - Published Police in Toronto are investigating after a gunshot was fired at the US consulate in the city - the second time this year such an incident has happened. Early on Monday morning, an officer stationed outside the consulate building heard the sound of a single gunshot and noticed a white car without a licence plate fleeing the scene. Police briefly engaged in a high-speed car chase before ending it over safety concerns. No injuries were reported in the incident. It is unclear how many individuals were involved in the attack. Monday's shooting comes after Toronto police arrested three people for a similar incident in March, which investigators have linked to a broader gun-for-hire network. Toronto police said they were investigating the latest attack with the help of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) and international law enforcement partners. Supt Jonathan Ko with the RCMP called it "another troubling incident", while the city's mayor, Olivia Chow, called the attack "brazen". "I want to say to the person or persons responsible: We will get you," Chow added. The shooting occurred around 04:45 local time (09:45 BST). Officers said they recovered one shell casing at the scene and damage to the building's facade. At least two individuals were inside the consulate at the time, Toronto Police Deputy Chief Frank Barredo said, but he noted the building is "very heavily fortified" and those inside likely did not hear the gun shot. He added that the investigation remains ongoing and that police across the city have been asked to look out for the potential suspects. "We will bring the people responsible to justice," Barredo said. In a post on X, the US consulate in Toronto thanked the police for their response. Police have been stationed outside the consulate since March, when shots were fired outside the building in what police at the time called a "national security incident". No one was injured in that attack. In June, police carried out raids in relation to the shooting. Police officer Marc Pinizzotto, 43, was killed during the operation. Police later arrested several suspects aged 18 and 19 for allegedly carrying out a string of shootings, including the March attack outside the consulate, as part of a larger gun-for-hire network. Two Jewish-owned bakeries in the city were also targeted, at least one by gunfire, over the weekend. Police said on Monday there was currently nothing to link the two incidents, but they did not rule out a connection. "I'm totally disgusted by the shootings and vandalism that took place in Toronto over the last few days," Ontario Premier Doug Ford said. Prime Minister Mark Carney, meanwhile, said he was "appalled" and added: "Law enforcement has my full support as they conduct a thorough investigation and hold those responsible to account." In May, US officials arrested an Iraqi national, 32-year-old Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, for allegedly planning more than a dozen attacks in North America and Europe targeting Jewish institutions and US interests, including the one at the US consulate in Toronto. Police in Toronto have not said if al-Saadi is linked to their investigation, and they have not specified a motive for this latest consulate shooting.

item.title: Japan earthquake: What we know so far
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgewgxlpj3po?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Japan earthquake: What we know so far - Published Japan is reeling from the latest major earthquake to hit the country. Nineteen people are missing at an Aeon shopping centre and a paper factory after the 6.8 magnitude earthquake hit Kyushu island, an official said. The quake has also caused power cuts, damaged roads, collapsed a castle wall and destroyed a footbridge. Information is still coming out of Japan but here is what we know so far. When and where in Japan was the earthquake? The quake hit the Kumamoto prefecture on Kyushu island at 16:27 local time (07:27 GMT) on Tuesday, with hundreds of thousands of people being told to move to evacuation shelters. The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) reported the earthquake had a magnitude of 7.1, which the US Geological Survey later measured as a 6.8. Quake magnitude figures are often updated as seismologists obtain and analyse new data. Kumamoto - where the collapsed Aeon Mall is located - is a city on the Kyushu island of Japan. The southern island of Kyushu is the third-largest of the four main islands in Japan, and the second most populous. The Kumamoto prefecture is no stranger to earthquakes. A total of 278 people were killed in 2016 by powerful quakes in Kumamoto and neighbouring Oita prefectures, according to Japan's public broadcaster NHK. What happened at the shopping centre? People remain trapped inside an Aeon Mall in Kumamoto prefecture, the fire service said. Ten people remain unaccounted for at the shopping centre, an official at the Disaster Management Division of Kumamoto prefecture told the BBC. Four people have been rescued from the mall and their lives are "not in danger", the official added. A witness reported seeing an explosion and smoke at the shopping mall after the quake. The witness saw the second floor of the building collapse, with some shoppers taken to hospital. Japan's fire and disaster management agency later confirmed that the second floor of a "commercial facility" collapsed, with many people trapped inside. Where else has been affected? Elsewhere in the Kumamoto prefecture, a chimney reportedly collapsed at Nippon Paper's Yatsushiro Plant, according to police, who are being cited by NHK. An aerial photograph of the site obtained by Reuters news agency appears to show a broken and collapsed chimney. The disaster management official told the BBC that two people at the plant had been found in a state of "cardiac arrest" and nine people are still missing. Tremors also caused historic walls at the 17th-century Kumamoto castle to tumble. It is not the first time the castle has succumbed to an earthquake. When a 7.3 magnitude quake hit the region in 2016, parts of the 400-year-old castle were also damaged as turrets and curved walls collapsed. A footbridge also collapsed in the Kumamoto region. It is unclear if anyone was injured, or when the collapse took place. Traffic appears to be travelling on the bridge that runs parallel to it. More than 40,000 households are without power, according to an update on Kyushu Electric's website. There has also been damage to roads. There have been more than 60 aftershocks ranging in magnitude from 1 to 4, Japan's Meteorological Agency said. A tsunami warning was issued immediately after the quake, but was lifted within two hours.

item.title: 'It's a hell of a situation': Spain grapples with devastating wildfires
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c235m71mrreo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'It's a hell of a situation': Spain grapples with devastating wildfires - Published For the past week, firefighters have been tackling a series of wildfires ravaging the Spanish countryside, threatening dozens of communities and forcing more than tens of thousands of people to evacuate their homes. Three fires in the Madrid region have caused particular concern, with a new heatwave expected to hit Spain from Wednesday, fuelling fears that firefighting efforts could be hindered. "It's a hell of a situation," said Madrid regional leader Isabel Díaz Ayuso, as she visited affected areas on Monday alongside Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez. Sánchez spoke on Tuesday of highly challenging hours and days ahead, but of light beginning to appear "at the end of the tunnel". Temperatures are expected to approach 40C in some regions in the coming days, with the heatwave forecast to last at least until Sunday. Spain's state meteorological agency Aemet has warned the "fire danger level will continue to rise to extreme levels, hindering firefighting efforts". Regional authorities began lifting some evacuation and lockdown orders on Tuesday as conditions improved - including in parts of the Madrid region - but restrictions remain in place in the worst-affected areas. In the Madrid region alone, more than 56,500 people have been evacuated since the fires broke out last week. A further 27,797 people have been ordered to stay at home. Further evacuations have taken place in Ávila, Toledo and Valencia. Ayuso had earlier described the wildfires as "the biggest natural catastrophe in the history of Spain". She wrote on X that the situation was now "improving little by little" and some residents may soon be allowed to return home. Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told Spain's La 1 TV channel that firefighting efforts on Monday night had resulted in "relatively positive progress". "This morning, we are very satisfied with the work done. We are going to consolidate the work that has been done," he said. He maintained that "we must be positive; we have the emergency under control" but conceded that "weather conditions are not helping us at all". Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced on Tuesday that areas affected by the wildfires have been declared "disaster zones". "The climate emergency is worsening year after year, and we are required to be united to fight against fire, as well as in prevention and reconstruction," he told reporters during a briefing in Madrid. "Therefore, I make an explicit request, a single appeal to all regional governments: Climate denial is the worst fuel for the fight against the climate emergency." Spanish journalist Juan Navarro, who is in Cebreros - a town around 40 miles west of Madrid – told the BBC that people were looking with fear to the next heatwave. When you drive through villages in the area around Cebreros, "everything is black", he said. The mayors of two of the evacuated towns in the Madrid region described the fire as "a kitten by night and a lion by day". Robledo de Chavela mayor Fernando Casado said his community would continue fighting "with their knives out". Echoing his sentiments, Valdemaqueda mayor Ricardo Meneses added that "we can't let our guard down and we're on high alert because now is the time to stop the fire". A psychologist visiting shelters has told El Mundo there is a growing sense of anxiety among the evacuees. "We've seen cases of people who come in relatively relaxed on the first day because they think this situation might only last a day," said Sara Casado, of the Citizen Services Department of the Madrid region. "But then they see how the hours and days go by. That uncertainty of being here without knowing when they'll be able to return increases their anxiety." The Madrid region is currently under a red weather warning, with temperatures expected to reach 35C in mountainous areas and 38C in other parts of the community. In its latest update, the national government's delegation in Madrid said the fire "remains active and uncontrolled". "Today's efforts will focus on surveillance and cooling the affected areas in anticipation of the forecast worsening of weather conditions," it added. Around 77,000 hectares (190,000 acres) have been affected by the fires in Spain, according to the minister for ecological transition, Sara Aagesen. The wildfire burning in the Ávila area was the largest in the country's recent history, she added. In Ávila, where more than 50,000 hectares have burned down since the start of the wildfires, the government's representative said the fire had a "quite favourable" evolution overnight. Nicanor Sen, however, said there had been "small flare-ups" that were now being monitored by emergency services. Meanwhile, the government of Valencia lifted a lockdown order for the town of Vall D'Uixo after a fire broke out of 25 July, forcing some 16,000 from 20 municipalities to evacuate. However, the local council's fire department representative, David Vicente, told the press on Tuesday afternoon that the fire remains "very active". In neighbouring Portugal, firefighters are tackling a large fire on three active fronts in the eastern Guarda area. The Portuguese Institute for Sea and Atmosphere (Ipma) has put large parts of the country under a very high red fire alert, with some areas under the highest warning level.

item.title: A Japanese town wrestles with identity after protests over its first mosque
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c36d79nd5w8o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
A Japanese town wrestles with identity after protests over its first mosque - Published Today, it's a field of grass. But soon, it'll be the site of the first mosque in this Japanese town. "It makes me worry about how our community might change," says long-time resident Noriko Izumizawa. Plans to build an Islamic religious site in Fujisawa, a laid-back seaside town about an hour's drive south of Tokyo, have sparked a wide range of emotions. There is anger and fear, as well as hope and acceptance, exposing the growing anxieties over immigration and social change as Japan grapples with a labour shortage from a shrinking and ageing population. Although immigration remains politically sensitive and restrictive, Japan is increasingly relying on foreign workers to fill open jobs. That means an influx of immigrants with various cultures, languages, religions and ways of being. So the debate that is playing out in towns like Fujisawa across the country is one that goes to the heart of how Japan sees itself. Izumizawa is not alone in the way she feels. She is among a group of Fujisawa residents who are anxious about the increasingly visible Muslim community. She says that the polarising debates around immigration in the US and Europe have also contributed to her unease. Earlier this year, anti-mosque protests flared up at the local train station, where thousands took to the streets to object to the proposed construction of the mosque. Some argue that a mosque much larger than the nearby Japanese Shinto shrine is disrespectful. There have also been reports of hate speech and misinformation spreading on Japanese social media. Local outlets say mosques have been receiving abusive phone calls and emails, some of which has prompted anti-hate groups to organise counter protests calling for no hate. Hiroki Suzuka, who manages a coffee shop opposite the road where the Fujisawa mosque is set to be built, calls for greater understanding and dialogue. "I'm not particularly opposed, but I wouldn't say I'm strongly in favour either," Suzuka said. "I think the first step is to learn about them, what Islam is, what kind of people they are, and what values and perspectives they hold. It begins with having an open mind and a desire to understand each other." Being Muslim in Japan Businessman Mohamed Mohideen has lived in Osaka for the past 39 years. He moved from his home country Sri Lanka in 1987 for better work opportunities during the economic bubble. He has dealt gemstones and later worked in trade, exporting used cars to countries like Sri Lanka and Pakistan. He moved at a time, he says, when there were far fewer foreign residents. But Mohideen feels that compared to back then, local people have become hostile and started making hurtful remarks at Muslims, both online and in person. "On social media, there are countless comments like, 'Get out of Japan' and 'Go back to your own country,'" Mohideen said. "People have also started coming to the mosque and shouting abuse." Mohideen goes to the Osaka mosque every day for prayers and other duties as a member of the local Islamic community. He says he has never felt that his life was in danger. Despite having good relationships with neighbours for many years, Mohideen has noticed the shift in attitude towards Muslims more recently. "Now, I feel that people are afraid of us." The verbal abuse has worsened in recent years. He recalled members of his Muslim community being called terrorists, accused of making bombs, and being told to get out of Japan. "When that happens, the only thing we can do is be patient. They're trying to provoke a fight or create a confrontation. They want to see how long we'll tolerate it," Mohideen explained. "So we stay calm, speak gently, and treat them kindly, because Japanese people generally don't know much about Islam." Still, he thinks there is some shared responsibility for the rift. "We focused only on our work and, for a long time, didn't make enough effort to help people understand who we are. We also didn't do enough to become part of the society," he said. "From now on, I want to work harder to increase dialogue and build better mutual understanding." Shakeel Mohamed, 61, has been representing the Yashio mosque in Saitama prefecture for the past decade. He had worked as a construction site supervisor for 26 years after moving to Japan from Pakistan and speaks fluent Japanese. Mohamed says the most important thing is to follow Japan's rules, including sorting refuse properly, obeying parking laws, and wearing helmets when riding your bicycle. "We make every effort to respect the way things are done in Japan and to follow the rules," he said. "Courtesy is important too, even something as simple as greeting people." He said Japanese locals in Yashio refer to the area's Pakistani community as "Yashio-stan". "Of course, there are some Pakistanis who behave badly, but they're only a small minority. And the same is true of Japanese people." Immigration vs identity Japan is wrestling with its identity in the face of huge demographic shifts. Muslims in Japan, including foreign residents and Japanese believers, numbered roughly 420,000 at the end of 2024, up from 230,000 in 2019, according to Hirofumi Tanada, a professor emeritus at Waseda University who studies the faith in Japan. The country's growing Muslim population also reflects a greater nationwide trend. The foreign resident population – which mainly comes from China, Vietnam, South Korea and the Philippines - surpassed four million in 2025. A record 2.57 million of them work in Japan, according to government data. In the same year, Japan's population declined by nearly 1 million. Government officials have long avoided describing the country as an immigration country, but push visas that are seen as more temporary than permanent. Critics describe this as a "stealth" immigration system. But even then, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has adopted a highly conservative stance against large-scale immigration. In June 2026, the Japanese government decided to raise visa fees for foreign nationals fivefold, after not having increased the amount for nearly 50 years. Now, the government is planning to increase the number of employees at the Immigration Services Agency by about 230 people, aiming to strengthen enforcement against foreigners illegally overstaying. Officials may also introduce a limit to manage the number of foreign residents in the country. As immigrant communities become more visible, the country is being forced to confront a question it has long tried to avoid: Can Japan become a more diverse country while preserving its sense of identity and cohesion that it values? Back in Fujisawa, Izumizawa admits she has never had a negative experience with a Muslim neighbour herself. "The truth is, maybe I just fear the unknown," she shrugs. Additional reporting by Chie Kobayashi

item.title: As the US pauses the war with Iran, is Trump really running out of weapons?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0qvnk2ezp7o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
When US President Donald Trump took the stage earlier this month at the Pennsylvania Defense and Innovation Summit, flanked by the CEOs of some of America's largest defence firms, he had one message in mind: build more weapons, and build them faster. "We have the best quality in the world," Trump told the armsmakers gathered at the US Army War College, with 'Secretary of War' Pete Hegseth at his side. "But we need a little more speed." The Trump administration framed the summit as part of a two-pronged approach to revitalise American industry and bolster US warfighting capabilities and, in Hegseth's words, its "arsenal of freedom". Largely unspoken, however, was the vast expenditure of sophisticated and difficult-to-manufacture weapons used during nearly 40 days of intense combat operations in Iran during Operation Epic Fury earlier this year and tit-for-tat strikes that have taken place since. So far, the US government says the war has cost $37.5bn (£28bn), and the vast majority of that has been spent on munitions. By the time a tenuous ceasefire took effect on 8 April, US forces had struck over 13,000 targets across Iran, according to the White House. American air defences intercepted over 1,700 Iranian drones and ballistic missiles over the same period. Now, the US has paused its strikes on Iran to allow negotiations to go ahead. A New York Times report says that Trump was advised to shelve plans to escalate the conflict as it would further drain American stockpiles. On Monday, Trump denied there was a shortfall, telling the Wall Street Journal: "We have far more munitions than anyone in the world, and far more than we need." This has been a touchy subject for some time within the US administration. Last month, when pressed on the subject, Hegseth denied that supplies were thinning out. His position seems to have changed since. Last week, he told the Senate Appropriations Committee that the Pentagon needed another $87bn (£68bn) to address "critical shortfalls", including equipment. Exact ammunition expenditures and remaining stockpiles remain classified. But publicly available data compiled by the Washington DC-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) paints a stark picture of depleted stockpiles that, in the short-term, are difficult to replace. "It depends on the munition - but one to five years [to make a single missile] is the bottom line," says Mark Cancian, a retired Marine Corps colonel and senior adviser at CSIS who has been researching the issue. "And there's nothing you can do to speed that up." But is the US really eating through ammunition so fast that it may struggle to fulfil its military duties and objectives? A depleted US arsenal The critical munitions used in the war span two categories: long-range ground attack systems, and the air and missile defences used to intercept incoming Iranian attacks. Among the ground attack systems that saw the greatest use was the Tomahawk Land Attack Missile - or TLAM - that is typically fired from ships or submarines at targets that could be well over 1,000 miles (1,600km) away. These weapons allow the US to conduct precision strikes against hardened military targets, such as command bunkers or fortified military facilities, without putting manned aircraft in harm's way. More than 1,000 Tomahawks have been fired during the war, the CSIS estimates, and the stockpile may not return to pre-war levels until 2031. According to the CSIS, the latest variants of the TLAM cost about $2.6m (£2m) per missile. Of the air defence systems used in the war, the most heavily used was the Patriot, a ground-based missile used to target aircraft, as well as ballistic and cruise missiles. According to the CSIS estimate, as many as 1,430 were used during the conflict from an estimated pre-war stockpile of about 2,330. Each Patriot interceptor costs approximately $4m - an expensive but effective option repeatedly used to shoot down Iranian drones that themselves only cost between $20,000-50,000 each. These will be hard to replace. "It takes several years to produce a missile. If you put money into the system today, you wouldn't get a missile for three or four years. Sometimes even five," Cancian says. "What we're getting [now] are missiles that were funded in 2023." Also used was a newer, more sophisticated system known as Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, which has a longer range and higher intercept altitudes than the older Patriot. Supplies were already limited, with CSIS estimating that between 190 and 290 were fired out of an estimated pre-war stock of 360. With only nine THAAD batteries operational in the world - and seven of them American - sustained expenditure could leave US forces without a system that would be critical to defending ballistic missile threats from countries such as Russia, China or North Korea. All eyes on Taiwan and the Pacific The war with Iran comes just before what is often referred to as the "Davidson window", in which a Chinese effort to invade Taiwan becomes, in the eyes of some US military planners, more likely. The controversial concept - which is central to US military thinking in the Pacific - stems from a 2021 congressional hearing in which Admiral Philip Davidson, then in charge of US forces in the region, warned that an invasion would happen "in the next six years". In 2023, then-CIA director William Burns predicted China would be ready to invade by 2027. China has long vowed to "reunify" with self-governing Taiwan, which it views as a breakaway province, and has not ruled out the use of force. Whether or not the US will defend Taiwan and go to war with China is a hotly debated topic. Despite the ambiguity, the US provides the island with defensive weaponry. Cancian refers to the munitions shortfalls as a "window of vulnerability" in which the US "is not going to have the depth of the preferred munitions it needs" if there is a conflict in the Pacific. This, he believes, increases the risk of US forces being left unprepared to face a vast arsenal of Chinese missiles and aircraft it could bring to bear in a Pacific conflict. China - which US officials say has been closely studying US air defences in the Iran war - has invested heavily in missile technology in recent years, including hypersonic glide missiles far more sophisticated than the missiles and cheap drones used by Iran. Beijing has also heavily invested in developing massive "drone-swarm" tactics. However, not everyone views the depleted US stockpiles as purely a liability. Jacob Olidort, a veteran of the CIA and former adviser on Middle East Policy in the Office of the Secretary of Defense, points out that using these weapons in combat also sends a powerful message. "Weapons create deterrence, not merely because nations have them, but also because they demonstrate a willingness to use them," said Olidort, now director for American security policy at the conservative-leaning America First Policy Institute. He adds that US "successes at eroding Iran's military capabilities with precision, with record time, send a signal to other adversaries, including China and their ambitions." What about Europe? The apparent tension between arming allies and preserving US reserves is one that has already been played out over Ukraine. Back in October 2025, months before Operation Epic Fury began, Trump declined to give Ukraine Tomahawks, citing a need to avoid depleting US stockpiles. The episode was a preview of the trade-offs now shaping the post-Iran debate over the wider arsenal. Ukrainian officials say they urgently need Patriots and other air defence systems to stem wave after wave of Russian drone and missile attacks. "In addition to energy prices, it [the Iran war] means the depletion of US reserves, and the depletion of air defence manufacturers," Zelensky told the BBC in March. "So we [Ukraine] have a depletion of resources." Zelensky put numbers to the concern: the US produces roughly 60 to 65 missiles a month, or between 700 to 800 a year, with 803 used on the first day of the Operation Epic Fury alone. More recently, however, Trump surprised many European officials by offering to give Ukraine the right to produce Patriots domestically. Similar arrangements already exist in Germany and Japan. Elaine McCusker, a 13-year veteran of the Department of Defence who now works as an expert with the American Enterprise Institute, says Ukraine's experience fighting Russia - as well as the US experience fighting Iran - could help create cheaper, mass-produced systems to complement existing high-ticket items. "We've known for a long time that we don't want to be shooting $6m interceptors at $1,000 drones," she says. "I think we now have more focus on that solution, and more people focusing on manufacturing more attritable solutions that don't cost so much". The aftermath Despite it all, there is little near-term alarm about the prospect of munitions running out - not because US stockpiles are unlimited, but because Iran's are in far worse shape. "The United States military has more than enough munitions, ammo, and stockpiles to serve all of President Trump's strategic goals and beyond, and Operation Epic Fury has exposed what happens when you mess with the United States," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement sent to the BBC. "Even still, the president has urged our defence contractors to constantly produce more made-in-America weapons," she added. Recent strikes announced by US Central Command have been largely focused on degrading Tehran's ability to threaten ships in the Strait of Hormuz, the vital shipping lane that Iran and the US have blockaded. Iran's military losses have been far greater than America's following wave after wave of US and Israeli strikes - and the country has extremely limited ability to address those shortages anytime soon. "A lot of commentary portrays Iran as having an almost unlimited amount of weaponry," says Jason Brodsky, policy director of United Against Nuclear Iran. "I think we have to realise that there are limitations there, and that the US has degraded their defence industrial base to a very significant extent," he says. He adds that Iran's "capacity to produce, at scale, the kinds of missiles, drones and other weapons systems" it needs has been largely destroyed. More from InDepth - The dark side of the Brazilian butt lift boom - Published6 July
Iran's remaining stockpiles, according to Brodsky, are being funnelled towards what he termed Tehran's trump card - its ability to threaten the Strait of Hormuz. In his view, it is a fading capability. "The Iranian regime is running out of time here." The current, manageable conflict with Iran - what Brodsky called the US military's "centre of gravity" takes immediate precedence for Washington, even as officials acknowledge it would be "irresponsible" to ignore the broader stockpile picture. "The Indo-Pacific is a more distant threat right now," he says. "Policymakers have to prioritise, and the Middle East right now has the president's attention." For now, every missile fired at an Iranian target, sent to Ukraine's frontlines or held back for Taiwan, comes from a pool that has steadily shrunk. Despite this, Washington is betting it can get through this conflict while production catches up. item.title: China's new challenge as natural disasters strike - fake AI videos
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx27mjvxgg1o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
China's new challenge as natural disasters strike - fake AI videos - Published As China deals with the fallout of Typhoon Noul that made landfall over the weekend, officials will be painfully aware that they will likely have an additional challenge to deal with: dangerously misleading videos created with Artificial Intelligence (AI). Powerful storms and flooding incidents over the last few months have seen fake videos inundating social media platforms – these include images of dead bodies floating in floodwaters, the false depiction of severe flooding in areas actually not affected and others with blatantly fake details of emergency response efforts. In some areas, videos containing false information about power outages prompted residents to panic buy emergency supplies. Other videos capitalise on real-life incidents. Flooding in Hengzhou city, Guangxi in early July caused hundreds of snakes to escape from a breeding farm. Then fake images were also published showing crocodiles being released into a river. In an already tense and dangerous situation involving mass evacuations and complex rescue operations, authorities want to avoid panic. Now they fear that AI technology - which China is pouring billions of dollars into - is providing simple, accessible tools that can be used to trick the public. "Many of these content creators use disaster news to try to gain followers, knowing that more sensational or exaggerated content will garner more likes and more views. They are deliberately fabricating information to grab people's attention," Huang Zhihua, Deputy Chief in charge of online public security for Zhejiang Police Department told Chinese state media. In recent weeks, there have been arrests and punishment – ranging from detention awaiting criminal prosecution to fines – for the creation of bogus reports and video content. But experts are warning that an unprecedented crisis of misinformation could be looming. In an article published by the newspaper of the Communist Party's Central Party School, Professor Chen Bin said, "AI dramatically lowers the technical barriers to producing false information. Individuals no longer require sophisticated technical skills. By simply prompting AI tools, they can rapidly generate convincing text, images, audio and video… which is highly realistic but entirely fabricated content, manufactured on a large scale." Professor Gao Fuping, from the East China University of Political Science and Law, told the BBC that motivation for the publishing of such false content ranges from those who do it "to create something amusing without thinking about the consequences", to those who want to "generate traffic for personal gain" or those who wish to deliberately "cause panic or social unrest". "Some users think the online world is anonymous and unregulated or that they cannot be traced," he said. There have been calls for all AI-generated content to be clearly stamped but other users can then just re-edit the material removing the markings. Professor Xu Xiaoke from Beijing Normal University told the BBC that greater efforts were also needed to verify geographic locations with timestamps and the checking of image sources. "That said, I would also stress that detection technology still lags behind generation technology. We're in a constant cat-and-mouse game. So we should not assume that technology alone can identify AI-generated content with the click of a button," he warned. The Chinese government is embracing AI in its bid to become the leading tech superpower. In 2017, it announced that AI would be "the main driving force" of the country's progress. Vast sums of money is pouring into AI businesses seeking more capital, fuelling domestic competition. The state-controlled wire service Xinhua reports that the country has over 6,000 "AI companies". In this climate, Prof Xu believes that China needs to build "trusted information infrastructure". This could include official government early warning systems and disaster interfaces which news organisations can access. But there have been instances of official sources, including government-controlled media, deliberately downplaying disasters, which has led to some public mistrust in this area. Earlier in July, local journalists were asked to "soften" their language to describe a major breach in the wall of the Liulan Dam near Naning as an "opening" or "gap". Officials appeared to be trying to make the breach sound less alarming but the consequences were deadly. Water bursting through the broken dam led to at least 26 deaths downstream. And this is not an isolated incident. In 2021, local officials were arrested, accused of concealing or underreporting 139 deaths in Henan province. Incidents like these have resulted in a trust vacuum that has made it much easier for bad actors to spread fake content. But police are imploring people to trust accredited sources during emergencies. "When encountering disaster-related information from an unknown source, approach it with scepticism and rely on official announcements," Gao Kai from the Ningbo Public Security Bureau said. He also tried to reassure the public that the creators of false information would be caught, saying that "the internet is not a lawless zone. Public security authorities will continue to intensify efforts to crack down on illegal online activity". "We've created a specialised task force to monitor social media closely, especially short video platforms. They will investigate and handle these cases quickly, cracking down in a very strict manner". Punishment could range from a fine to up to seven years in prison if the fallout of the misinformation is serious enough. On 23 July, China's Cyberspace Administration also announced a nationwide crackdown on fake internet content related to floods and other disasters, ordering its local branches to focus on catching out fabricated data, malicious editing, staged scenes, misattributed historical events and those impersonating officials. In addition, it called on social media platforms to strengthen the review of the content they are publishing. Prof Gao believes "the answer is public education combined with law enforcement", saying that there was a "need to publicise real cases where people have been punished." He added that "the harm caused by AI-generated fake content is ultimately the result of how people choose to use the technology - not the technology itself", adding that existing laws were sufficient to deal with it. However, others are not so confident. Professor Chen pointed out that "AI technology continues to evolve much faster than legal frameworks. As new legal questions emerge, AI misinformation remains a considerable challenge." Shanghai and Washington based lawyer Peter Pang says lawyers around the world are seeing an explosion in the number of cases dealing with these issues. He believes that the companies that create AI apps and the platforms used to publish fake videos and other material must be held legally accountable along with the people who create misinformation. "The first line would be the platforms, because they're the ones that are the enablers. They're the ones that allow this to go out," he told the BBC. He used a hypothetical example of a person who runs over a pedestrian following panic induced by a fake post on social media. "The video creator might say 'you ran over somebody. That's your problem. I didn't do it.' But let's think it through. You created the foundation from which people reacted. If you created that panic, you need to have responsibility for consequences that occur." And Professor Xu warns that "AI-generated misinformation is likely to increase not only in volume but in the speed with which it spreads." "Looking ahead, political elections, public health emergencies, armed conflicts, natural disasters and issues affecting people's livelihoods are all likely to become high-risk areas for AI-generated misinformation. "Instead of waiting for false information to go viral before trying to contain it, governments and platforms should now be preparing in advance." - Published7 July

item.title: European wildfires in maps - and how they're being tackled
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj638jx0l53o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Devastating European wildfires in maps - and how they're being tackled - Published Wildfires are tearing through France and Spain, forcing more than 300,000 people to evacuate their homes. France has seen its worst fires in two decades, while officials in the Spanish capital Madrid say they are the worst the region has ever experienced. It follows a sweltering summer of heatwaves across Europe that have seen temperatures soar above 40C (104F) in many places. Wildfires in the regions outside Madrid have burned about 254 sq miles (660 sq km) since 1 July, authorities estimate - an area larger than the city itself. In France, the worst affected area is Gironde, around the city of Bordeaux, where more than 200,000 people have been forced from their homes. The blaze has spread rapidly, tearing through forests and fields in France's famous wine region, and burning more than 162 sq miles (420 sq km) in less than four days - an area roughly four times the size of Paris. It is now just nine miles (15km) from the south of Bordeaux. The fires have also threatened a number of sensitive military and industrial sites in the area, including facilities that work on French ballistic missiles, rocket motors, and the processing of hazardous chemicals. The fires have become so extreme they have created their own giant fire thunderstorm. A rare weather event, storms like these are formed when heat from the wildfires makes the air above the fire rise rapidly, carrying smoke, ash and water vapour high into the atmosphere. As the air rises, it cools, and the water vapour condenses into a cloud. If the fire is powerful enough and the atmosphere is unstable, that cloud can grow into a cumulonimbus - the same type of cloud associated with thunderstorms. If these clouds then become large enough, they can produce their own lightning, which can then start new fires. They can also occasionally bring hail and rain. These extreme and unpredictable conditions make the fires all the more difficult to stop. To combat them, French firefighters have been using planes loaded with fire retardant, as well as planes like the Canadair, which can scoop 6,000 litres of water from lakes or the sea in 12 seconds and drop it directly on the fires. On dangerous days, loaded aircraft patrol high-risk areas before any fires have been reported, so they can drop within minutes of a sighting. Planes often fly in a continuous shuttle while retardant is laid along the edges of the fire and ground crews attack the flames directly. 1 of 3 In Gironde, about 2,500 firefighters, 1,500 military personnel, and 1,200 police officers and gendarmes have been involved in tackling the blaze. But even with these numbers, Gironde official Jean Luc Gleyze told the BBC that authorities don't have enough people to combat the fires. "We don't have enough people and enough trucks and even I think France don't have enough," he said. Around the town of Lacanau, bulldozers, diggers and mechanical shovels have been used to carve a firebreak that is 100m (328ft) wide at points, according to French media. A firebreak is essentially a stretch of land that has been stripped of all vegetation to stop the fire from spreading - removing any potential fuel before the fire has a chance to reach it. Spanish teams have been using many of the same techniques to tackle their wildfires, which are on course to become the worst the country has seen in two decades. Francisco Martin, a government delegate in Madrid, described one of the fires as "undoubtedly the largest fire in the history of the Madrid region". This summer's fires have been aided by the hotter, drier conditions caused by climate change, which allow fires to spread faster and burn more fiercely. Many on the ground - in both Spain and France - are fearful that the coming week could see worsening conditions, with high pressure forecast to bring dry, settled and increasingly hot temperatures. 1 of 5 Additional reporting by Elizabeth Rizzini and Helen Willetts.
